title: The poem and this text
short: Written 1797-8 and first printed in Lyrical Ballads (1798); this archive gives the revised text of 1817/1834 without its prose marginal gloss.
body: Coleridge began the poem in November 1797 on a walk over the Quantocks with William and Dorothy Wordsworth, and it opened Lyrical Ballads (1798) as 'The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere', in deliberately archaic spelling and diction. He modernised much of it for the 1800 edition and, for Sibylline Leaves (1817), added the Latin epigraph from Thomas Burnet and the prose gloss printed in the margins, which glosses the action in the voice of a pious antiquarian editor. Line references in these notes follow the standard 1834 numbering (625 lines); the text here, from Arthur Symons's 1905 selection, follows the later wording but omits both epigraph and gloss, and runs a few lines longer after about l. 300, so a printed line count may differ slightly from the reference given. Readers should know the gloss exists: many interpretations, for example of the Polar Spirit or the moon, lean on it, and some critics argue the gloss is a further fiction rather than the author's key.

title: one of three
short: The Mariner singles out one of three wedding guests, the bridegroom's kinsman; the frame sets his tale of isolation against a communal feast.
body: The frame narrative is a ballad device: an old man stops a young one on his way to a marriage, and the merriment inside the hall ('the loud bassoon', the bride 'Red as a rose') interrupts the tale. The guest is chosen, not random; Part VII says the Mariner knows at sight 'the man that must hear me'. Critics have read the pairing as setting two kinds of communion against each other: the social sacrament of marriage and the solitary religious experience the Mariner brings back. The poem ends with the Mariner preferring the walk 'together to the kirk' to the marriage-feast, and the guest turning away from the bridegroom's door, so the frame is changed by the tale.

title: glittering eye
short: The Mariner holds his listener by the eye, not the hand; the image draws on contemporary interest in mesmerism or 'animal magnetism'.
body: The guest throws off the 'skinny hand' but cannot resist the eye, and 'listens like a three years' child'. Coleridge was interested in Franz Anton Mesmer's 'animal magnetism', which was much discussed in Britain in the 1780s and 1790s, and editors have connected the fascinating eye with that vogue, as well as with the older folklore of the evil eye and the serpent's power to charm its prey. The eye recurs through the poem: the dying crew curse him 'with his eye', the dead men's eyes fix on him, and the poem ends with the Mariner 'whose eye is bright'. Looking, cursing and blessing are tied together throughout.

title: loon; Eftsoons
short: 'Loon' means a worthless fellow or lout; 'eftsoons', already archaic in 1798, means 'at once, forthwith', a Spenserian word.
body: Coleridge's ballad diction mixes genuine old words with pseudo-medieval colour. 'Loon' (Scots and northern English) is a rogue, idler or simpleton. 'Eftsoons', literally 'soon after', had dropped out of ordinary use by the seventeenth century but was familiar from Spenser's Faerie Queene, where it is frequent. Other archaisms in the poem include 'wist' (knew), 'ken' (see, know), 'clomb' (climbed), 'uprist' (rose up), 'shrieve' (absolve after confession) and 'trow' (believe). The 1798 version carried far more of this archaic spelling, and early reviewers, Southey among them, found the poem strange and obscure, which partly explains Coleridge's revisions of 1800.

title: like a three years' child
short: Wordsworth claimed to have written this line and the next; the guest is reduced to a child's helpless attention.
body: In the Fenwick notes of 1843 Wordsworth recalled that he supplied two or three lines near the opening, including 'And listened like a three years' child: / The Mariner had his will' (he misdates the walk to spring 1798). Coleridge himself acknowledged a debt to Wordsworth for two lines in Part IV ('As is the ribbed sea-sand') in a footnote in Sibylline Leaves. The simile makes the hold of the tale almost hypnotic: an adult wedding guest becomes a small child who cannot choose but hear. It also anticipates the poem's closing simplicity, a moral fit for a child, which some critics take at face value and others regard as deliberately inadequate to what has been told.

anchor: The sun came up upon the left
title: The sun came up upon the left
short: The sun's position charts the voyage: rising on the left, the ship sails south; in Part II it rises on the right, after rounding Cape Horn into the Pacific.
body: Coleridge never names places, but the sun gives exact bearings. Sailing south from Britain, a ship has the rising sun on its left (east). The storm drives it to the polar ice; after the Albatross guides it out, the sun rises 'upon the right' (Part II), so the ship is now heading north up the Pacific side of South America. 'Higher and higher every day, / Till over the mast at noon' marks the approach to the equator, where the becalmed ship lies under a sun directly overhead. Lowes traced how Coleridge assembled this geography from his wide reading of travel and voyage literature, including Cook's voyages and accounts of the southern ice.

anchor: At length did cross an Albatross
title: Albatross
short: The idea of the bird came from Wordsworth, who had read in Shelvocke's Voyage (1726) of an albatross shot off Cape Horn.
body: Wordsworth told Isabella Fenwick that he proposed the crime that brings spectral persecution on the Mariner: he had been reading Shelvocke's Voyage Round the World, where the second captain, Simon Hatley, shot a black albatross that had followed the ship in bad weather, believing it an ill omen. Wordsworth suggested the killing and the tutelary spirits who avenge it. The bird is hailed 'As if it had been a Christian soul', fed by the crew, and greeted 'in God's name'; it thus becomes a guest and almost a fellow Christian, which makes its killing a violation of hospitality as well as of nature. Whether it is a symbol (of Christ, nature, or the spirit of love) or simply a creature is a long-running debate.

title: With my cross-bow / I shot the Albatross
short: The killing is given no motive; critics read it as the type of a gratuitous original sin, an act of will against nature, or simply a meaningless act.
body: The stanza withholds a reason: the guest asks why the Mariner looks so stricken, and the answer falls abruptly into the last line of Part I. The absence of motive is the poem's central crux. Robert Penn Warren, in his influential 1946 essay, read the act as a re-enactment of the Fall, a crime of the perverse will against the 'One Life', with the moon and the wind as symbols of the imagination. Empson resisted the Christian scheme, reading the poem instead as an expression of guilt over European maritime expansion and the slave trade. Jerome McGann argued that the poem's layered texts and gloss deliberately present a history of interpretation rather than a single meaning. Students should notice that the crew's verdicts on the act shift with the weather (Part II), complicating any simple moral reckoning.

title: For all averred
short: The crew first condemn the killing, then, when the fog clears, approve it, so becoming accomplices; their judgement follows only their luck.
body: 'Averred' means declared, affirmed. In two balanced stanzas the sailors call the Mariner a wretch for killing the bird 'That made the breeze to blow', then, when the sun rises 'like God's own head', say it was right to kill birds 'That bring the fog and mist'. The marginal gloss of 1817 makes the point explicit, saying the crew thus make themselves accomplices in the crime. The repetition shows a morality based on consequences and superstition; it also explains, within the poem's logic, why the whole crew die while the Mariner, the principal, is left to a worse fate of living on.

title: Water, water, every where
short: The most quoted lines of the poem, often misquoted ('and not a drop to drink'); the crew die of thirst surrounded by undrinkable sea-water.
body: The repetition imitates the endless view of salt water, and 'all the boards did shrink' shows the ship's planks shrinking in the heat. The paradox of thirst amid water had a long history in sea narratives, but Coleridge's plain ballad phrasing made it proverbial; the usual misquotation smooths away his abrupt 'Nor any drop to drink'. Spiritually, the image fits the poem's pattern of deprivation in the midst of plenty: the dead calm is a drought of grace as well as of water, ended in Part V only after the Mariner blesses the water-snakes and the rain falls.

anchor: slimy things did crawl with legs
title: slimy things did crawl with legs
short: The 'very deep did rot': the sea seems to putrefy and breed loathsome creatures, which the Mariner will later learn to bless.
body: Lowes connected these images with descriptions in voyage literature of the becalmed sea seeming to stagnate and of marine organisms swarming at the surface. At this stage the creatures are disgusting to the Mariner, 'slimy things'; in Part IV he still sees 'a thousand thousand slimy things' that live on while his comrades die. The turn of the poem comes when he sees the same sea-creatures, the water-snakes, as beautiful and blesses them 'unaware'. The language of slime and rot thus measures his spiritual condition rather than the creatures themselves.

title: Instead of the cross, the Albatross / About my neck was hung
short: The crew hang the dead bird on the Mariner in place of the cross, a mark of guilt; the image gave English the idiom 'an albatross round one's neck'.
body: The cross a sailor might wear as a sign of salvation is replaced by the sign of his crime; the rhyme of 'cross' and 'Albatross' (already linked in 'did cross an Albatross') presses the association between the bird and Christ, which Christian readings exploit. The image recalls the custom of hanging a dead animal on a dog that has killed livestock. It is reversed at the end of Part IV, when the Mariner prays and 'The Albatross fell off, and sank / Like lead into the sea'. The modern idiom for a burdensome guilt or encumbrance derives from this passage.

title: Death and Life-in-Death
short: A skeleton ship carries Death and a female 'Night-mare Life-in-Death', who dice for the crew; she wins the Mariner, Death the rest.
body: The spectre-ship that sails without wind is a hulk of bare ribs through which the sun peers 'as through a dungeon-grate'. Its crew are two allegorical figures. The woman, with red lips, golden hair and skin 'white as leprosy', combines erotic allure with disease, a 'Night-mare' in the old sense of an incubus that sits on the sleeper. Her prize is the condition the Mariner then endures: alive, but unable to pray or to die. The 1798 version describes Death more grotesquely, as a skeleton with jet-black bones; Coleridge cut the passage in later editions. The dicing echoes medieval and ballad imagery of Fortune and of soldiers casting lots.

anchor: The horned Moon, with one bright star
title: The horned Moon, with one bright star / Within the nether tip
short: A crescent moon with a star inside its horns is astronomically impossible, since the star would lie behind the moon; the omen announces the crew's deaths.
body: Sailors held a star 'dogging' the moon to be an ill omen, and the 1817 gloss calls it so. Commentators since the nineteenth century have pointed out that no star could appear within the dark part of the moon's disc, since the moon would hide it; some see a deliberate supernatural sign, others a slip. Lowes found possible sources in astronomical reports and in Coleridge's reading, and he cited records of apparent 'stars' seen within the moon's crescent. Either way, the moon is one of the poem's governing presences, presiding over the curse here and over the Mariner's release in Part IV.

title: long, and lank, and brown, / As is the ribbed sea-sand
short: The guest compares the gaunt, sun-browned Mariner to sand ridged by the tide; Coleridge credited these lines to Wordsworth.
body: In Sibylline Leaves Coleridge added a footnote acknowledging that he owed these two lines to Wordsworth, whose other contributions to the poem's early shape he recalled in the Fenwick note (without mentioning these lines). 'Ribbed' describes the ripples left in sand by receding water, and it also suggests the ribs of an emaciated body, and the 'ribs' of the spectre-ship through which the sun peered. The guest's renewed fear pauses the narrative at the start of Part IV, reminding the reader that the man speaking survived, and the Mariner's reply ('This body dropt not down') introduces his solitary ordeal.

anchor: a curse in a dead man's eye
title: a curse in a dead man's eye
short: Worse than an orphan's curse, the look of the dead men keeps the Mariner from prayer for seven days and nights; he cannot die.
body: An orphan's curse was proverbially powerful, since orphans had God as their protector (compare the biblical commands to defend the fatherless, as in Exodus 22:22-24). The Mariner sets the dead men's silent curse above it. The number seven, the length of the curse, has scriptural resonance as the days of creation and of mourning. The stanza is six lines long, extending the ballad quatrain as the ordeal is prolonged; 'And yet I could not die' states the Life-in-Death condition. The release depends on the moon's rising in the next stanzas and on the blessing that follows.

anchor: The moving Moon went up the sky
title: The moving Moon went up the sky
short: The rising moon, gently personified, introduces the turn; the 1817 gloss on this stanza is one of the most celebrated passages of Coleridge's prose.
body: The stanza is in calm contrast to the stasis before it: the moon moves and 'no where did abide', with a star or two beside her. In Sibylline Leaves Coleridge's marginal gloss here describes the Mariner, in his loneliness, yearning towards the journeying moon and the stars, which still sojourn yet still move onward and are everywhere at home. Warren made the moon and its light the symbol of the imagination and of grace throughout the poem. Under the moonlight the sea outside the ship's shadow looks like hoar-frost, while the water in the shadow 'burnt alway / A still and awful red'.

title: the water-snakes ... I blessed them unaware
short: The turning point: seeing the sea-creatures as beautiful, the Mariner blesses them spontaneously; he can pray, and the Albatross falls from his neck.
body: The 'slimy things' of Part II are now 'happy living things' with 'rich attire' of blue, green, velvet black and golden fire. The blessing comes 'unaware', from 'A spring of love' rather than an act of will, and the poem attributes it equally to 'my kind saint'. Warren read the moment as the operation of grace, answering the gratuitous crime with a gratuitous act of love, and many critics connect it with Coleridge's idea of the 'One Life' in all creatures. Notice the exact reversal of the earlier failure: in Part IV he 'tried to pray' but a 'wicked whisper' dried his heart; now 'The selfsame moment I could pray'. The release is partial, though, and penance continues.

title: silly buckets
short: 'Silly' here probably means empty, useless, or simple; its older senses 'blessed' and 'innocent' fit the stanza's mood of grace.
body: The word has puzzled readers. Its root, Old English sǣlig, meant 'happy, blessed' (compare German selig), and over centuries it came to mean innocent, simple, helpless, and finally foolish. Coleridge's buckets have stood empty and useless through the drought, and editors gloss 'silly' as 'useless' or 'empty', while noting the older sense of 'blessed', apt for buckets now to be filled by heaven-sent rain. The stanza turns the dream into fact: the Mariner dreams the buckets are full of dew, and wakes to rain. Sleep is attributed to 'Mary Queen', in keeping with the poem's Catholic medieval setting.

title: Two voices in the air
short: Two spirits discuss the Mariner: the first recalls the Polar Spirit's love for the bird, the second says the man 'hath penance done, / And penance more will do'.
body: The Polar Spirit that 'bideth by himself / In the land of mist and snow' has driven the ship from beneath; the 1817 gloss calls him one of the invisible inhabitants of this planet, neither departed souls nor angels, and cites Josephus and the Platonist Michael Psellus as authorities on such daemons. The second voice, 'soft as honey-dew', is gentler and introduces the idea of penance, the Catholic sacramental sequence of contrition, confession and satisfaction that the Mariner's later shriving by the Hermit continues. The line 'He loved the bird that loved the man' compresses the poem's chain of love between creatures.

anchor: Like one, that on a lonesome road
title: Like one, that on a lonesome road
short: A simile of a traveller who dares not look back because a fiend follows him; Mary Shelley quotes the stanza in Frankenstein.
body: The spell broken, the Mariner still dreads what is behind him, and the simile gives his state the shape of folk fear: the walker who has once turned round, seen something, and walks on without daring to look again. The stanza was quickly famous. Mary Shelley has Victor Frankenstein quote it as he flees through Ingolstadt after creating his creature (vol. I, ch. 4 in 1818; ch. 5 in 1831), and her novel elsewhere echoes the Rime through Walton's polar voyage and Victor's isolation. Coleridge, a friend of her father William Godwin, had recited the poem in the Godwin household when she was a child, according to family tradition.

title: the Hermit good ... He'll shrieve my soul
short: The Hermit is the poem's priestly confessor; to 'shrieve' (shrive) is to hear confession and absolve, washing away 'The Albatross's blood'.
body: Arriving in the Pilot's boat, the Hermit lives in the wood by the sea, kneels on a moss-covered stump, and loves to talk with sailors from far countries. He stands for an unworldly, nature-loving piety that the poem treats with affection. 'Shrieve' is the Middle English form of 'shrive', from Old English scrīfan, to impose penance. When the Mariner begs 'O shrieve me', the Hermit's demand 'What manner of man art thou?' forces the tale out of him; the confession brings relief, but not final absolution, since the agony returns 'at an uncertain hour' and compels him to tell the story again and again.

anchor: I have strange power of speech
title: I pass, like night, from land to land
short: The Mariner is compelled to wander and retell his tale; critics have read him as an image of the poet, or of the Wandering Jew.
body: The penance never ends: an agony returns at uncertain hours, and he must find the one listener who 'must hear me'. The image of the wanderer passing 'like night, from land to land' recalls the legend of the Wandering Jew, condemned to wander until the Second Coming, which Coleridge knew and to which Lowes and later critics compare the Mariner. Many readers also see an image of the poet, driven to speak and gifted with a 'strange power' that holds his audience, and some biographical critics link the Mariner's guilt and isolation with Coleridge's own. The tale itself is a 'teaching' ('To him my tale I teach'), which leads into the poem's much-debated moral.

anchor: He prayeth best, who loveth best
title: He prayeth best, who loveth best
short: The plain moral of love for all creatures; Coleridge later said the poem had too much moral, not too little, as Mrs Barbauld had complained.
body: In Table Talk (31 May 1830) Coleridge recalled that Anna Laetitia Barbauld told him the poem's faults were that it was improbable and had no moral. He replied that it had too much moral, and that its chief fault was the open intrusion of the moral sentiment into a work of pure imagination; it ought to have had no more moral than the Arabian Nights tale of the merchant whose thrown date-shell puts out the eye of a genie's son, so that the genie claims his life. Critics divide: some take the closing stanzas as the poem's sincere centre, others think the neat moral is the Mariner's inadequate reduction of an experience that exceeds it, since the tale's punishments far outrun the crime and include innocent men.

anchor: A sadder and a wiser man
title: A sadder and a wiser man
short: The guest, stunned and 'of sense forlorn' (bereft of his senses), never goes in to the feast; he wakes next morning sadder and wiser.
body: The poem ends not with the Mariner but with his listener, who turns from the bridegroom's door 'like one that hath been stunned'. 'Forlorn' here has its older sense of 'deprived of, lost'. The last couplet suggests that the tale's knowledge is a kind of fall: wisdom comes with sadness, as in Ecclesiastes 1:18 ('he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow'). The frame thus repeats the poem's pattern of isolation from community, though now as a beginning of understanding rather than as a curse. The phrase became proverbial.

sources.cite: The Holy Bible, Authorized (King James) Version (1611), Ecclesiastes 1:18
